Start: a double bar with dots (or a start-of-line brace), the C3 clef and three sharps. Then a single beamed group of five notes on the same pitch, which reads as E4, before the first barline. This fits the tail of bar 70: E4 16th, E4 8th, E4 8th, E4 8th, E4 16th. That is five repeated E4s, and the first and last notes carry an extra flag or stroke, matching the 16ths. So the line opens partway through bar 70. The opening 16ths and the D#4 8ths were on the previous line.

The next two groups are higher (A4 ×8). The fourth group is lower (F#4 ×4). The long-beamed groups sit higher still: they are the two B4 quarter tremolos written out as 16 32nds. That is bar 71.

Third stretch, after the second barline: four groups of four 32nds on one low pitch (E4 ×16). That is the first half of bar 72. The line ends with a wavy sign (a custos or abbreviation mark) and no closing barline. The second half of bar 72 (the two E4 quarter tremolos) is either abbreviated here or carried to the next line. Either way the line ends in bar 72.

Nothing contradicts the edition. The only uncertainty is the exact pitch of the opening group, which can't be confirmed beyond 'repeated notes near the E4 line'.
insights: Bars 71 and 72 were easy to match. The copyist writes out the tremolos as 32nd groups, so the contour E–A–A–F#–B×4 and then the run of repeated E's are distinctive. The hard part was the opening fragment of bar 70: five repeated eighth-like notes after what looks like a repeat sign, with the 16th flags hard to see. Seeing the end of the previous line, or the edition's rhythm at the bar 70 split, would settle it.
